title: The Critic That Teaches a Sampler
summary: Goodfellow et al. turn generative modeling into a two-player game whose ideal equilibrium matches the data distribution without requiring an explicit likelihood or Markov-chain sampling.
objectives: Define the generator, discriminator, latent prior, and model distribution.
Reconstruct the minimax objective and its alternating optimization process.
Derive the optimal discriminator for a fixed generator.
Explain why matching the data distribution minimizes the ideal objective.
Distinguish the ideal theorem from guarantees about practical neural-network training.

sections.title: The estimation problem is turned sideways
sections.markdown:
A generative model should produce samples distributed like observed data. Let $\bm{x}$ denote a data-space sample and let $p_{\text{data}}(\bm{x})$ denote the unknown distribution that produced the training examples. A traditional likelihood-based method asks the model to assign usable probabilities to observations. Goodfellow et al. instead propose learning through discrimination: make generated samples, ask another model to distinguish them from data, and send its gradient back into the generator.

The two learned functions have different jobs. The generator $G(\bm{z};\theta_g)$ maps a noise vector $\bm{z}$, drawn from a chosen prior $p_{\bm{z}}$, into a synthetic sample. Its parameters are $\theta_g$. Repeated sampling and mapping induce a distribution $p_g$ over $G(\bm{z})$ even when no tractable formula for $p_g(\bm{x})$ is available. The discriminator $D(\bm{x};\theta_d)\in[0,1]$, with parameters $\theta_d$, estimates the probability that $\bm{x}$ came from the data rather than $G$.

This is the paper's particular conceptual move: a classifier supplies the learning signal for an implicit sampler. It does not mean the discriminator is the final product, nor that $G$ reconstructs each training example. After training, generation is simply a draw of $\bm{z}$ followed by a forward pass through $G$.

sections.title: Noise becomes a distribution through a map
sections.markdown:
The prior $p_{\bm z}$ supplies the generator with variability. A draw $\bm z\sim p_{\bm z}$ is mapped to data space by $G(\bm z;\theta_g)$, and the distribution of those mapped samples is $p_g$. In this sense, $G$ reshapes probability mass: latent regions with greater prior probability, or regions that the map sends to similar outputs, contribute more mass to the corresponding parts of the model distribution. This defines a sampler even though the model does not provide an explicit normalized value for $p_g(\bm x)$ at an arbitrary point.

The figure examines this prerequisite geometry with a constructed isotropic Gaussian prior, $\bm z\sim\mathcal N(\bm 0,\sigma^2 I_D)$. Because

$$
\mathbb E\lVert\bm z\rVert^2=D\sigma^2,
$$

its root-mean-square radius is $\sigma\sqrt D$. Here $D$ is the number of latent coordinates and $\sigma$ has the same units as each coordinate, so the radius is measured in latent-space units. At $D=4$ and $\sigma=0.5$, for example, the RMS radius is $0.5\sqrt4=1$. This is a declared illustrative calculation rather than a parameter reported by the paper.

Changing $\sigma$ rescales every sampled vector: doubling $\sigma$ doubles both the norm distribution's horizontal scale and the reference RMS radius. Changing $D$ instead changes how many squared coordinates contribute to each norm, moving the characteristic radius according to $\sqrt D$ and altering the histogram's relative spread. The measured mean norm shown by the figure need not equal $\sigma\sqrt D$, because the latter is $\sqrt{\mathbb E\lVert\bm z\rVert^2}$ rather than $\mathbb E\lVert\bm z\rVert$.

This calculation clarifies what the noise input contributes to the adversarial method: it is a distribution of starting points whose mass is transformed by the learned map, not a single fixed seed. The Gaussian choice belongs to the constructed exercise; the framework itself only requires a chosen noise prior, and the generator—not the latent norm alone—determines the resulting distribution in data space.

sections.title: Reading the two-player objective
sections.markdown:
The value function is

$$
\min_G\max_D V(G,D)=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}\sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(\bm{x})]+\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}\sim p_{\bm{z}}}[\log(1-D(G(\bm{z})))].
$$

Here $\mathbb{E}$ means an average under the indicated distribution. The discriminator maximizes both terms. On real $\bm{x}$, a larger $D(\bm{x})$ raises $\log D(\bm{x})$. On generated $G(\bm{z})$, a smaller discriminator output raises $\log(1-D(G(\bm{z})))$. The generator minimizes the second term because the first contains no generated sample; it tries to move its outputs toward values that $D$ labels as real.

A small illustrative calculation clarifies the signs. Suppose one real example receives $D(\bm{x})=0.8$ and one generated example receives $D(G(\bm{z}))=0.25$. Their discriminator score is $\log 0.8+\log 0.75=\log 0.6\approx-0.511$. If the discriminator improves the assignments to $0.9$ and $0.1$, the score becomes $\log 0.9+\log 0.9=\log 0.81\approx-0.211$, which is larger, as discriminator maximization requires. These numbers are illustrative and are not experimental measurements.

The word “simultaneously” describes one coupled game, not literal same-instant parameter writes. The proposed numerical procedure alternates $k$ discriminator steps with one generator step; the reported experiments used $k=1$.

sections.title: Why the generator sometimes needs a different loss
sections.markdown:
The formal minimax generator minimizes $\log(1-D(G(\bm{z})))$. Early in training, however, generated samples may be easy to reject. When $D(G(\bm{z}))$ is near zero, this expression is in a saturated region and can provide a weak learning signal. The paper therefore suggests training $G$ to maximize $\log D(G(\bm{z}))$. This non-saturating alternative pushes generated samples toward higher “real” probability and has the same stated fixed point, while supplying stronger early gradients.

The optimizer figure isolates one prerequisite behind this discussion. It performs ordinary gradient descent on the invented scalar function $f(x)=x^2/2$, starting at $x=3$, for 12 updates. Because $f'(x)=x$, a learning rate $\eta$ gives $x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta x_t=(1-\eta)x_t$. With the illustrative choice $\eta=0.25$, $x_1=2.25$ and $x_2=1.6875$. Use the control to predict whether larger steps approach zero faster or begin to oscillate.

This toy exposes how gradient magnitude and step size govern numerical progress, but it is deliberately not GAN training: it has one convex objective, one scalar parameter, and no alternating opponent. Real adversarial training changes each player's objective landscape as the other player changes.

sections.title: Solve the discriminator before judging the generator
sections.markdown:
The theoretical analysis first freezes $G$, hence freezes $p_g$, and optimizes $D$. At one location $\bm{x}$, write $a=p_{\text{data}}(\bm{x})$ and $b=p_g(\bm{x})$. The discriminator's pointwise contribution is

$$
a\log y+b\log(1-y),
$$

where $y=D(\bm{x})$. When $a>0$ and $b>0$, the optimum is interior: differentiating gives $a/y-b/(1-y)$, and setting this to zero yields

$$
D_G^*(\bm{x})=\frac{p_{\text{data}}(\bm{x})}{p_{\text{data}}(\bm{x})+p_g(\bm{x})}.
$$

The zero-density cases are boundary optima rather than stationary points. If $a>0$ and $b=0$, maximizing $a\log y$ gives $D_G^*(\bm{x})=1$. If $a=0$ and $b>0$, maximizing $b\log(1-y)$ gives $D_G^*(\bm{x})=0$. These cases agree with the same density-ratio formula wherever $a+b>0$. When $a=b=0$, the point lies outside the combined support and the objective does not constrain $D(\bm{x})$.

Every symbol is local and interpretable: $D_G^*$ is the best discriminator for fixed $G$; the numerator is real-data density; the denominator is total density from the equally represented real and generated sources in the criterion.

For an illustrative discrete point with $p_{\text{data}}(\bm{x})=0.3$ and $p_g(\bm{x})=0.1$, the optimum is $0.3/(0.3+0.1)=0.75$. If the two densities are equal and nonzero, it is $1/2$. Thus $D=1/2$ at equilibrium does not mean the discriminator learned nothing. Under the ideal analysis, it means the sample's source cannot be inferred because the two distributions agree.

sections.title: The equilibrium theorem—and its boundary
sections.markdown:
Substitute $D_G^*$ into the value function and call the result $C(G)=\max_D V(G,D)$. The paper rewrites it as

$$
C(G)=-\log 4+2\,\operatorname{JSD}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_g),
$$

where $\operatorname{JSD}$ is the Jensen–Shannon divergence. It is nonnegative and equals zero only when its two distributions agree. Consequently, the global minimum is $-\log 4$, achieved uniquely in distribution space at $p_g=p_{\text{data}}$. At that point, the optimal discriminator outputs $1/2$ wherever the shared distribution has support.

A common misconception is that this theorem guarantees that any neural GAN trained by alternating gradient steps will converge. It does not. The convergence proposition assumes enough capacity, an optimal discriminator for the current generator at every step, and sufficiently small improvements to $p_g$ in the non-parametric distribution space. The implemented generator instead represents a restricted family through $G(\bm{z};\theta_g)$ and updates parameters $\theta_g$. The paper explicitly notes that this introduces multiple critical points and removes the theoretical guarantee.

The theorem therefore identifies the desired ideal equilibrium and validates the population objective. It is not a certificate for finite data, finite networks, noisy minibatches, or practical optimization trajectories.

sections.title: Evidence, tradeoffs, and what remains unresolved
sections.markdown:
The paper trained models on MNIST, the Toronto Face Database, and CIFAR-10. It presented generated samples and estimated test-data probability using Gaussian Parzen windows fitted to generated samples, selecting the Gaussian width by validation. The reported table gives an MNIST estimate of $225\pm2$ and a TFD estimate of $2057\pm26$ for adversarial nets, under the table's dataset-specific procedures. Those values should not be detached from their estimator: the authors warn that it has high variance and performs poorly in high-dimensional spaces. They also make no claim that their displayed samples surpass existing methods.

The framework's computational attraction is direct sampling by forward propagation, without a generation-time Markov chain. Its corresponding cost is that $p_g(\bm{x})$ is not explicitly represented. Training also requires coordination: if $G$ moves too far while $D$ becomes stale, its gradients may cease to provide a useful current comparison. The paper specifically warns about collapsing many latent values to the same output, which sacrifices diversity.

These boundaries matter. The lesson and cited results do not establish claims that depend on unspecified architecture, optimizer, or preprocessing choices. Nor do the results establish universal convergence, calibrated likelihood evaluation, or dominance over other generators. The durable contribution is narrower and more important: a differentiable discriminator can train an implicit generator through an adversarial game, with a precisely characterized ideal solution.

options.text: The ideal distribution-space criterion has its unique global minimum at $p_g=p_{\text{data}}$ under the stated assumptions.
options.explanation: Correct. This matches the non-parametric result with an optimal discriminator and sufficient capacity.

options.text: Every finite neural GAN trained with minibatches must converge to the data distribution.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The theorem does not guarantee convergence for finite parameterized networks or practical optimization.
